conventions: be-eyney with a following rectum, where the ASV renders the phrase by a single evaluative adverb, is one fused unit of the preposition and ayin under rules 30 and 40, headed on the construct noun, while the rectum keeps its own English and is aligned separately. JDG.14.3 (be-eynay to 'well', suffix to 'me') and JDG.14.7 (be-eyney Shimshon to 'well', Shimshon to 'Samson'). Do not split the pair and do not mark the preposition unrepresented beside a noun holding the whole word: no English word in the phrase renders ayin's own lexeme, so rule 40's subtraction test finds the noun's rendering gone with the adverb.

An intensifying adverb the ASV writes beside a Hebrew verb's own English word belongs to that verb's unit and does not move the head off the lexical verb: tsalach to 'came mightily' heads on 'came' (JDG.14.6, JDG.14.19) and hetsiq to 'pressed ... sore' heads on 'pressed' (JDG.14.17), the unit discontinuous around the object under rule 25. Rule 44's light-verb clause does not reach these, because the English verb is the lexical predicate and not a light verb; rule 44's surplus-particle sentence does not either, because the adverb renders force the source verb's own stem carries rather than something the Hebrew leaves unwritten.
report: Read the dump end to end and all 52 candidate lemma groups. No cross-verse split found: every multi-treatment bucket is licensed either by a different source morpheme standing in the clause or by different English the ASV actually wrote. Ledger re-checked from the dump itself: 585 units, 583 source and 708 target ids each partitioned once, 8 added, matching the validation report.

Constructions that recur and agree: be-eyney fused on the single 'well' in 14.3 and 14.7, headed on ayin, with the rectum (suffix in 14.3, Samson in 14.7) keeping its own word; tsalach to 'came mightily' headed on 'came' in 14.6 and 14.19; ba-yom ha-shevi'i divided identically in 14.15, 14.17 and 14.18, the assimilated article taking the phrase's one written 'the' and the agreement article unrepresented under rule 47; eshet Shimshon and beit avi- recast as English possessives with the rectum holding the possessive in 14.15, 14.16, 14.19 and 14.20; the presentative hayah frame's 'that' on the apodosis waw in 14.11, 14.15 and 14.17; the supplied object 'it' added in 14.12, 14.13 and twice in 14.16.

Differences checked one by one rather than assumed, and each licensed by the source: the directive he is aligned wherever the ASV writes a directional word (14.1 'to', 14.5 'to', 14.18 'down') and unrepresented wherever another morpheme already holds the relation (14.1 and 14.2 beside a written be-, 14.5 beside the rectum's 'of'); lo plus yakhol fuses on the indivisible 'cannot' in 14.13 and splits in 14.14 where the ASV wrote 'could not', which is what rule 35 directs in each case; ha- plus participle gives 'the eater' its written 'the' in 14.14 while the anarthrous az beside it takes 'the strong' whole under rule 46; every dative le is unrepresented where the ASV wrote no preposition for it and aligned where it did, verse by verse.

The two most hedged units are 14.6's supplied 'he had', marked added on rule 43's count (no hayah, the be- spent on 'in', the suffix spent on 'his', and ayin already rendered by the fused 'nothing', so rule 43's subtraction leaves nothing diminished), and 14.18's 'down' given to the Sd rather than read as the verb's phrasal particle, which rule 32's closing sentence and rule 11's priority for a present morpheme both direct. Both carry the competing reading in their notes; neither conflicts with anything elsewhere in the chapter.

BSB: all 37 disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors. The bulk are the directive he (3), datives and other prepositions the ASV recasts away under rule 40 (18), object markers under rule 16 (4), and articles the ASV leaves unwritten under rules 29, 41 and 47 (7). Of the five singletons, 14.13's paragogic he is named by rule 32 as exactly this convention gap; 14.9's waw and 14.11's waw are clauses the ASV recast with no connective; 14.9's second possessive suffix is rule 22's unrendered repetition, the ASV writing one 'his' for both nouns; and 14.12's infinitive absolute is unrepresented because the ASV wrote no intensifier for it, 'can' being the finite verb's modal under rules 17 and 56.

One edge I would revisit only if the chapter were reopened for other reasons, and did not change here: 14.9's 'on' in 'went on eating as he went' is kept with the finite verb as a phrasal particle, though the continuation it writes is arguably what the infinitive absolute halokh already carries in its own 'as he went'. It is defensible as accepted and re-cutting it would not be a consistency fix.
